title: We Greet You, Salma, So Greet Us
intro: Abu Tammam placed this poem near the start of the chapter on valour, the first in his anthology the Hamasa, under the heading “one of the Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba”; his commentators al-Marzuqi and al-Tibrizi add that it is also given to Bashama al-Nahshali, and al-Baghdadi, in Khizanat al-Adab, judges that attribution correct. Its authorship is much disputed: al-Mubarrad gives most of these lines to a man of the Nahshal clan called Abu Makhzum, whom a note in one manuscript of his book identifies as Bashama ibn Hazn; Ibn Qutayba gives them to Nahshal ibn Harri; al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi has the first two in a short poem by al-Muraqqish the Elder; and Abu Muhammad al-A'rabi held that two poems had been run together, the line “We, the sons of Nahshal” being Bashama's and other lines, the opening among them, al-Muraqqish's. It opens by greeting a woman called Salma, which al-Marzuqi reads as a way into the boast, then praises the clan's lineage, its lead in every race for honour, the unbroken line of its chiefs, its readiness to spend lives in war and wealth on blood money, and its composure in grief. Al-Marzuqi says that, looked at closely, “each of them is a peak that calls you to itself, in wording and meaning”, and grammarians cite them, Ibn al-Sarraj for the accusative of “the sons of Nahshal” and al-Baghdadi for the word julla.

translation: We greet you, Salma, so greet us in return;
if you give drink to the noblest men, give drink to us.
1.sharh: He and his people greet a woman called Salma and ask to be greeted back, and to be given drink whenever she serves the noble, being noble themselves. Some read “give drink” as praying for rain.

translation: And if one day you call to a grave matter or a noble deed
the chiefs of the noblest men, then call on us.
2.sharh: If she ever summons the leading men to face a crisis or win honour, she should summon his people too. Al-Marzuqi notes that the greeting, the drink and the summons are only a way into the boast.

translation: We, the sons of Nahshal, disown him for no other father,
nor would he sell us for other sons.
3.sharh: The clan and its ancestor are content with each other: they would never claim another father, nor would he trade them for other sons. The Arabic sets “the sons of Nahshal” apart, as needing no introduction.

translation: If one day men race for some goal of honour,
you will find the winners and the runners-up are ours.
4.sharh: Whenever men compete for glory, the first and second to arrive are always his kinsmen. The image is a horse race: the musalli finishes second, its head at the winner's haunch.

translation: No lord of ours ever dies
without our having raised among us a boy to be lord.
5.sharh: Leadership never lapses in the clan: when a chief dies, a young man raised for the role takes his place, so they never need an outsider. Al-Mubarrad traces the thought to Abu al-Tamahan al-Qayni.

translation: On the day of terror we hold our lives cheap,
but were we asked to sell them in peacetime, they would be dear.
6.sharh: In battle they spend their lives as if they were worthless; in peace no price could buy them. Al-Marzuqi stresses that he means out of reach, not sold dearly, and admires the paired contrasts, cheap and dear, terror and peace.

translation: White are our partings, our cauldrons boil;
with our wealth we heal the wounds our hands have made.
7.sharh: Their heads are white at the parting, their cauldrons always boiling, and they pay blood money for those they wound rather than face revenge. The white partings may mean hair greyed by hardship, bald patches from helmets, or a clean name; al-Shantamari prefers paths worn white by guests.

translation: If one of us were among a thousand and they cried
“What horseman?”, he would think it was him they meant.
8.sharh: Any one of them, among a thousand strangers, would take a cry for a horseman to mean him, since, as al-Shantamari puts it, they are known as horsemen who defend. Al-Marzuqi rates this above Tarafa's similar line, since here one man stands out among a thousand.

translation: When champions shy away from the swords' edges,
we lengthen the blades with our own arms.
9.sharh: When even the bravest hang back from the swords, his people step forward until their blades reach the enemy, as if their arms lengthened them. Al-Mubarrad says the image comes from Ka'b ibn Malik.

translation: However great their loss, you never see them
weeping with the mourners over those who die.
10.sharh: However great the loss, they never weep with the mourners: death in battle is too familiar to break them. Al-Tibrizi adds that every child born among them grows up a chief, so they do not grieve.

translation: At times we ride into what men dread, and it is lifted
from us by our guarding of honour and by swords that serve us well.
11.sharh: Sometimes they plunge into dangers others shun, and their fierce defence of their honour and their trusty swords carry them through. Some read the swords as men as sharp as swords; al-Marzuqi and al-Tibrizi prefer real swords.

1.1.4.meaning: Salma: a woman's name; she is addressed in the first two lines only.

2.1.4.meaning: Julla: a grave matter, a great affair.

2.2.2.head: سَراة
2.2.2.meaning: Sarat: the chiefs and nobles of a people.

3.1.2-3.meaning: The sons of Nahshal: the clan of Nahshal ibn Darim, a large branch of the tribe of Tamim. Those who gave the poem to a man of Qays ibn Tha'laba read “the sons of Malik” instead.

3.2.5.head: شَرى
3.2.5.meaning: Sells us. The verb shara means both to sell and to buy.

4.2.4.head: المُصَلّي
4.2.4.meaning: Musalli: in a horse race, the horse that comes in second.

5.2.2.head: اِفتَلى
5.2.2.meaning: We weaned and reared, from the word for weaning a foal; al-Shantamari glosses it “we chose”.

6.2.6.head: أَغلى
6.2.6.meaning: They were found dear, or made dear: the subject is “our lives”, and the final a lengthens the rhyme.

7.2.1.head: أَسا
7.2.1.meaning: We heal, we dress a wound.

9.1.2.head: الكُماة
9.1.2.meaning: Kumat: champions, warriors hidden in their armour.

9.2.2.head: الظُّبات
9.2.2.meaning: Zubat: the edges or points of swords.

11.2.2.head: الحِفاظ
11.2.2.meaning: Hifaz: the defence of one's women and honour in war.
